questions.q: Which kind of system exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings?
questions.explain: In an isolated system neither matter nor energy crosses the boundary (e.g. an ideal thermos flask).

questions.q: Which of these is a state function?
questions.explain: U, H, S and G are state functions; q and w depend on the path.

questions.q: A system absorbs 701 J of heat and does 394 J of work. What is ΔU?
questions.explain: ΔU = q + w = +701 + (−394) = +307 J (w is negative when the system does the work).

questions.q: Which is true for an adiabatic process?
questions.explain: Adiabatic means no heat exchange (q = 0), so ΔU = q + w = w.

questions.q: An ideal gas expands isothermally into a vacuum. Then:
questions.explain: p_{ex} = 0 so w = 0; for an ideal gas ΔU = 0 so q = 0.

questions.q: A gas expands from 2 L to 10 L against a constant external pressure of 1 atm. What is w (work done on the gas)?
questions.explain: w = −p_{ex}ΔV = −1 × (10 − 2) = −8 L atm; the gas does the work.

questions.q: For an isothermal expansion between the same two volumes, which path lets the system do the most work?
questions.explain: In a reversible expansion the external pressure stays almost equal to the gas pressure, giving the largest area under the p–V curve.

questions.q: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), how are ΔH and ΔU related?
questions.explain: Δn_{g} = 2 − 4 = −2; ΔH = ΔU + Δn_{g}RT = ΔU − 2RT.

questions.q: Which quantity does a bomb calorimeter measure directly?
questions.explain: The bomb is sealed, ΔV = 0, so w = 0 and q_{V} = ΔU.

questions.q: A calorimeter with C = 20.7 kJ K⁻¹ warms by 1 K when 1 g of graphite burns (M = 12.0 g mol⁻¹). What is ΔU?
questions.explain: −20.7 kJ per gram; times 12.0 g mol⁻¹ gives −248 kJ mol⁻¹ (exothermic).

questions.q: What is the standard enthalpy of formation (Δ_{f}H°) of an element in its reference state at 298 K?
questions.explain: By definition Δ_{f}H° = 0 for an element in its reference state.

questions.q: From C + O₂ → CO₂ (−393.5 kJ) and CO + ½O₂ → CO₂ (−283.0 kJ), the ΔH for C + ½O₂ → CO is:
Δ_{f}H°: CaCO₃ = −1206.92, CaO = −635.09, CO₂ = −393.51 kJ mol⁻¹. What is Δ_{r}H° for CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂?
The atomisation enthalpy of CH₄ is 1665 kJ mol⁻¹. The mean C–H bond enthalpy is about:
questions.explain: Four C–H bonds: 1665 ÷ 4 ≈ 416 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: What lattice enthalpy does the Born–Haber cycle give for NaCl?
questions.explain: 411.2 + 108.4 + 121 + 496 − 348.6 = +788 kJ mol⁻¹ (energy is needed to separate the ions).

questions.q: In which process does entropy increase?
options: A gas condenses to a liquid
A solid melts to a liquid
A crystal is cooled to 0 K
questions.explain: On melting the particles become more disordered, so ΔS > 0.

questions.q: Which condition always holds for a spontaneous process?
questions.explain: Second law: the total entropy of system plus surroundings increases. ΔH or ΔS_{sys} alone does not decide.

questions.q: If ΔH is negative and ΔS is negative, the reaction is:
questions.explain: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; at low T the −TΔS term is small and the negative ΔH wins.

questions.q: With ΔH = +400 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +0.2 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, above what temperature is the reaction spontaneous?
questions.explain: Crossover T = ΔH/ΔS = 400/0.2 = 2000 K; above it ΔG < 0.

questions.q: If Δ_{r}G° is negative, what can be said about the equilibrium constant K?
questions.explain: Δ_{r}G° = −RT ln K; a negative Δ_{r}G° means ln K is positive, so K > 1.
